Partial cubes are graphs that can be embedded isometrically into hypercubes. In other words, a graph is a partial cube if the distance between any two of its vertices is the same as the distance between their images in some hypercube. This property makes partial cubes an important class of graphs in metric graph theory, since they combine combinatorial structure with geometric behavior similar to that of hypercubes.

Several fundamental structures play a central role in the theory of partial cubes, especially semicubes and the relations introduced by Djoković and Winkler. Semicubes arise from the way edges of a graph divide its vertex set according to distances from the endpoints of an edge. These sets are closely related to the coordinate structure of a hypercube embedding. Djoković’s and Winkler’s relations, defined on the edges of a graph, are used to identify which edges correspond to the same coordinate direction in a hypercube. Through these tools, one can analyze whether a graph has the metric properties required to be a partial cube.

The paper uses semicubes together with Djoković’s and Winkler’s relations to characterize both bipartite graphs and partial cubes of arbitrary dimension. These characterizations provide criteria for recognizing when a graph can be represented as an isometric subgraph of a hypercube. By working in arbitrary dimension, the results apply not only to finite-dimensional partial cubes but also to broader classes of graphs whose hypercube embeddings may require infinitely many coordinates.

In addition to presenting these characterizations, the paper offers new perspectives on several known results. Some previously established theorems are given new proofs using the framework of semicubes and edge relations. These proofs help clarify the underlying structure of partial cubes and show how different concepts in the theory are connected. The paper also introduces new characterizations, thereby extending the set of available tools for studying bipartite graphs and partial cubes.

The paper further examines several graph operations that preserve or generate partial cubes. Among these are the Cartesian product, pasting, expansion, and contraction. These operations make it possible to construct new partial cubes from known ones and to study how their structural and metric properties change. In particular, the paper uses these constructions to determine or estimate important invariants such as the isometric dimension and the lattice dimension of partial cubes. The isometric dimension measures the number of hypercube coordinates needed for an isometric embedding, while the lattice dimension concerns embeddings into integer lattices. Together, these operations and dimension calculations provide a systematic approach to building and analyzing partial cubes.

Partial cubes are graphs that can be embedded isometrically into hypercubes. In such an embedding, graph distances are preserved exactly: the distance between two vertices in the graph is the same as the Hamming distance between their corresponding binary vectors. Because of this close connection with hypercubes, partial cubes form an important class of graphs in metric graph theory, with applications in combinatorics, discrete geometry, lattice theory, and the study of networks.

This text develops a detailed study of partial cubes through several equivalent viewpoints and constructive methods. A central role is played by semicubes, which are the two complementary vertex sets determined by an edge according to which endpoint is closer to a given vertex. Semicubes provide a natural way to describe how a graph can be represented inside a hypercube, since each coordinate of a hypercube embedding corresponds to a partition of the vertex set into two such classes. The text also examines Djoković’s relation and Winkler’s relation, two fundamental relations on the edge set of a graph. These relations capture when two edges behave like parallel edges in a hypercube and therefore provide powerful criteria for recognizing partial cubes.

The work presents characterizations of bipartite graphs and partial cubes in terms of these relations and associated convexity properties. Since every partial cube is bipartite, the structure of bipartite graphs is especially important. The text discusses how the behavior of semicubes, convex cuts, and equivalence classes of edges can be used to determine whether a bipartite graph admits an isometric embedding into a hypercube. In particular, it gives new proofs and formulations of known criteria, while also establishing additional characterizations that clarify the relationship between graph distances, edge relations, and hypercube coordinates.

A major theme is the construction of new partial cubes from existing ones. The Cartesian product of graphs is one of the most natural operations in this setting: the Cartesian product of partial cubes is again a partial cube, and its hypercube representation can be obtained by combining the representations of the factors. This operation also has predictable effects on metric invariants, including the isometric dimension, which is the smallest dimension of a hypercube into which the graph embeds isometrically.

The text also studies pasting operations, where partial cubes are joined along suitable convex subgraphs. Under appropriate conditions, pasting preserves the partial cube property. This provides a useful way to build large and complex partial cubes from simpler pieces while retaining control over their metric structure. The analysis of pasting highlights the importance of convexity: if the common subgraph is convex in each component, distances remain well behaved after the pieces are glued together.

Another important construction is expansion. Expansions provide a systematic way to generate partial cubes by splitting part of a graph and inserting new edges between corresponding copies. This operation is closely related to the structure of semicubes and to the edge classes determined by Djoković’s and Winkler’s relations. Expansion is particularly significant because partial cubes can often be understood as arising from repeated expansions starting from a single vertex. In this way, expansion offers not only a method of construction but also a structural decomposition theorem for partial cubes.

Conversely, the text considers contraction operations. Contracting suitable classes of edges in a partial cube can produce smaller partial cubes while preserving essential metric information. Such contractions are naturally tied to the equivalence classes of edges that correspond to coordinates in a hypercube embedding. By contracting one coordinate class, one effectively removes a coordinate from the embedding. This gives a useful recursive approach to the study of finite partial cubes and helps explain how their dimensions and structural properties can be computed.

The text further investigates two important numerical invariants: the isometric dimension and the lattice dimension. The isometric dimension of a finite partial cube is the minimum number of hypercube coordinates needed for an isometric embedding. It is closely related to the number of equivalence classes of the appropriate edge relation. The lattice dimension, on the other hand, concerns isometric embeddings into integer lattices and reflects a different but related aspect of the metric structure. For finite partial cubes produced by Cartesian products, pasting, expansion, and contraction, the text describes how these dimensions can be calculated or bounded in terms of the dimensions of the constituent graphs and the operations performed.

Overall, the text provides a unified treatment of partial cubes through metric, combinatorial, and constructive perspectives. By using semicubes, Djoković’s relation, Winkler’s relation, Cartesian products, pasting, expansion, and contraction, it develops new characterizations and proofs for bipartite graphs and partial cubes. It also shows how important invariants such as isometric and lattice dimensions behave under standard graph operations. These results contribute to a deeper structural understanding of partial cube theory and offer useful tools for recognizing, constructing, decomposing, and analyzing partial cubes.

Partial structures are important in mathematics, computer science, and linguistics because they describe systems that are not fully defined or complete. Instead of assuming that every relationship, operation, or rule is available, partial structures allow some information to remain unknown, undefined, or intentionally limited. This makes them useful for modeling real-world situations, where data is often incomplete.

For example, in logic and model theory, a partial structure may contain functions or relations that are only defined for certain elements. In computer science, partial structures can help represent databases with missing values, unfinished programs, or systems that evolve over time. They provide a flexible framework for reasoning under uncertainty.

The name “Djokovi” may be associated with discussions of structure, strategy, or analysis, depending on the context. If referring to Novak Djokovic, one could make an analogy between partial structures and the way a tennis match develops. At the beginning of a match, the full outcome is unknown, and each point adds new information. Djokovic’s strategic style often involves reading partial patterns in an opponent’s game and turning incomplete information into effective decisions.

In this sense, partial structures are not simply incomplete objects; they are organized systems with meaningful gaps. Whether in mathematics, data analysis, or even sports strategy, understanding partial structures helps us interpret complex situations step by step.

counterfactuals.output: We present a unified study of structural and constructive aspects of partial cubes through the interplay of semicubes and the Djoković–Winkler relation. Starting from isometric embeddings of graphs into hypercubes, we characterize edge classes via the \(\Theta\)-relation and analyze the corresponding semicube decompositions as the fundamental coordinates of a partial cube. These tools are then used to revisit classical construction principles, including Cartesian products, isometric pasting along gated or convex subgraphs, expansions, and their inverse operations by contractions of \(\Theta\)-classes. We show how these operations preserve partial-cube structure under natural convexity and compatibility conditions, and we describe their effect on semicube systems and Djoković–Winkler equivalence classes. The resulting framework provides a coherent language for building, decomposing, and recognizing partial cubes, linking local edge relations with global hypercube embeddings. Several consequences for canonical representations, factorization, and recursive generation of partial cubes are discussed, illustrating the role of semicubes as both geometric separators and combinatorial coordinates.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a research article about characterizations of bipartite graphs and partial cubes using semicubes and Djoković's and Winkler's relations.
counterfactuals.output:
The article studies structural characterizations of **bipartite graphs** and **partial cubes** using the concepts of **semicubes** and the edge relations introduced by **Djoković** and **Winkler**.

A **partial cube** is a graph that can be embedded isometrically into a hypercube, meaning graph distances are preserved. Since hypercubes are bipartite, every partial cube is necessarily bipartite, but not every bipartite graph is a partial cube. The article focuses on identifying exactly when a graph has this stronger hypercube-like structure.

A central tool is the notion of a **semicube**. Given an edge \(ab\) in a connected graph \(G\), the two associated semicubes are typically defined as

\[
W_{ab}=\{x\in V(G): d(x,a)<d(x,b)\}
\]

and

\[
W_{ba}=\{x\in V(G): d(x,b)<d(x,a)\}.
\]

In bipartite graphs, every vertex lies in exactly one of these two sets, so the edge \(ab\) naturally separates the vertex set into two distance-based halves. In partial cubes, these semicubes behave like the two halfspaces determined by a coordinate hyperplane in a hypercube.

The article also uses two important relations on edges:

1. **Djoković’s relation**, often denoted \(\Theta\), where two edges \(ab\) and \(xy\) are related if

\[
d(a,x)+d(b,y) \neq d(a,y)+d(b,x).
\]

In bipartite graphs this relation captures when two edges behave as if they correspond to the same coordinate direction in a hypercube.

2. **Winkler’s relation**, a closely related relation often denoted \(\Theta'\), defined using distance inequalities such as

\[
d(a,x)+d(b,y) \neq d(a,y)+d(b,x),
\]

or equivalent formulations depending on orientation. In bipartite graphs, Djoković’s and Winkler’s relations coincide, but outside the bipartite setting they may differ.

A key theme of the article is that **partial cubes can be characterized by the behavior of these relations**. In particular, a connected bipartite graph is a partial cube precisely when Djoković’s relation is **transitive**, and therefore an equivalence relation on the edge set. The equivalence classes of this relation correspond to the coordinate directions of the hypercube into which the graph embeds.

The semicube viewpoint gives another characterization. For an edge \(ab\), the sets \(W_{ab}\) and \(W_{ba}\) should be convex: every shortest path between two vertices in the same semicube remains inside that semicube. This convexity mirrors the behavior of halfspaces in hypercubes. Thus, the article shows that a connected bipartite graph is a partial cube if and only if the semicubes determined by its edges are convex, or equivalently, if the Djoković/Winkler edge relation has the appropriate equivalence-class structure.

The article also clarifies the relationship between **bipartiteness** and these distance-based edge relations. Bipartite graphs have a clean separation property: for every edge \(ab\), vertices can be divided according to whether they are closer to \(a\) or to \(b\). This makes semicubes especially natural. However, to be a partial cube, the graph must satisfy additional consistency conditions: the semicubes must align globally so that the graph can be represented inside a hypercube.

Overall, the article presents several equivalent ways to recognize partial cubes:

- via isometric embeddings into hypercubes;
- via convexity of semicubes;
- via transitivity of Djoković’s relation;
- via equivalence classes of Winkler’s relation;
- via the interpretation of edge classes as hypercube coordinates.

The main contribution is to unify these perspectives and show how local distance comparisons around edges determine the global hypercube-like geometry of a graph.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you draft a mathematical paper abstract describing new characterizations and proofs for partial cubes, including operations for constructing new partial cubes from old ones?
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**  
Partial cubes—graphs that admit isometric embeddings into hypercubes—form a central class in metric graph theory, with connections to median graphs, CAT(0) cube complexes, chemical graph theory, and the theory of cut metrics. In this paper we present several new characterizations of partial cubes and give unified proofs based on the structure of Djoković–Winkler equivalence classes and convex edge cuts. We show that a connected bipartite graph is a partial cube precisely when its edge set admits a compatible system of convex semicube decompositions satisfying a local separation condition. This yields an intrinsic criterion that avoids explicit construction of a hypercube embedding and provides a streamlined proof of the classical isometric embedding theorem.

We also introduce new closure operations for constructing partial cubes from existing ones. These include convex expansion along gated or semicube-compatible subgraphs, cut amalgamation over matching convex boundaries, and controlled Cartesian and gated products. For each operation we prove that the resulting graph remains a partial cube and describe the induced behavior of its Θ-classes, semicubes, and isometric dimension. Conversely, we show that large families of partial cubes can be decomposed into smaller partial cubes by reversing these operations, giving recursive recognition and construction principles.

As applications, we derive simplified proofs of known results on expansions of partial cubes, obtain new decomposition criteria for finite partial cubes, and identify subclasses closed under the proposed operations, including median graphs and several classes of benzenoid-type graphs. The methods emphasize the equivalence between hypercube coordinates, convex cuts, and graph metric separation, and provide a flexible framework for producing and recognizing partial cubes without relying on an a priori embedding.

counterfactuals.output:
This paper develops a structural theory for partial cubes in arbitrary dimension, emphasizing the role of semicubes and their interaction with standard constructive operations such as Cartesian products, pasting, expansions, and contractions.

A central theme is the characterization of partial cubes through their isometric embeddings into hypercubes. For a partial cube, each coordinate of a hypercube embedding induces a pair of complementary convex vertex sets, called semicubes. The paper treats these semicubes as fundamental structural objects. Their incidence, intersection, and separation properties encode much of the metric and combinatorial behavior of the graph. In particular, the semicube system provides a coordinate-free way to analyze the Djoković–Winkler relation on edges and to understand how edge classes correspond to hypercube directions.

The paper also studies how partial cubes behave under Cartesian products. Since the Cartesian product of partial cubes is again a partial cube, product decompositions provide an important method for constructing and analyzing high-dimensional examples. The semicube structure of a product is shown to decompose naturally in terms of the semicube structures of its factors. This yields insight into dimension, convexity, and the organization of edge classes. Conversely, product factorization can often be detected from the arrangement of semicubes and their associated equivalence classes of edges.

Another major topic is pasting, where larger partial cubes are assembled from smaller ones along suitable convex subgraphs. The paper examines conditions under which such gluings preserve the partial cube property. Convexity plays a decisive role: pasting along convex intersections allows distances to remain compatible with hypercube embeddings. In this framework, semicubes help control how coordinates extend across the pasted components and how new global embeddings arise from local ones.

The paper further discusses expansion and contraction as inverse operations for generating and reducing partial cubes. Expansion splits a graph along an appropriate pair of convex or semicube-like substructures, introducing a new hypercube coordinate and thereby increasing dimension. Contraction reverses this process by identifying edges in a Θ-class, removing a coordinate while preserving the partial cube property under suitable hypotheses. These operations provide an inductive approach to arbitrary-dimensional partial cubes, generalizing classical expansion characterizations.

Taken together, the results present partial cubes as graphs governed by systems of convex cuts. Semicubes serve as the bridge between metric embeddings, combinatorial decompositions, and constructive operations. Cartesian products describe independent coordinate directions, pasting explains how partial cubes may be assembled along convex regions, and expansion/contraction methods provide a recursive mechanism for moving between dimensions. The paper thereby offers a unified framework for understanding the structure and construction of partial cubes beyond finite or low-dimensional settings.
